The Green’s function Monte Carlo combined with projected entangled pair state approach to the frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model

He-Yu Lin Address: Department of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China    Yibin Guo Address: CQTA, Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY, Platanenallee 6, 15738 Zeuthen, Germany    Rong-Qiang He Address: Department of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China    Z. Y. Xie Email: qingtaoxie@ruc.edu.cn Address: Department of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China    Zhong-Yi Lu Email: zlu@ruc.edu.cn Address: Department of Physics, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China Address: Key Laboratory of Quantum State Construction and Manipulation (Ministry of Education), Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China Address: Hefei National Laboratory, Hefei 230088, China
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The tensor network algorithm, a family of prevalent numerical methods for quantum many-body problems, aptly captures the entanglement properties intrinsic to quantum systems, enabling precise representation of quantum states. However, its computational cost is notably high, particularly in calculating physical observables like correlation functions. To surmount the computational challenge and enhance efficiency, we propose integrating the Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) method with the projected entangled pair state (PEPS) ansatz. This approach combines the high-efficiency characteristics of Monte Carlo with the sign-free nature of tensor network states and proves effective in addressing the computational bottleneck. To showcase its prowess, we apply this hybrid approach to investigate the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on the square lattice, a model notorious for its sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our results reveal a substantial improvement in the accuracy of ground-state energy when utilizing a preliminary PEPS as the guiding wave function for GFMC. By calculating the structure factor and spin-spin correlation functions, we further characterize the phase diagram, identifying a possible columnar valence-bond state phase within the intermediate parameter range of 0.52<J2/J1<0.580.52\textless J_{2}/J_{1}\textless 0.58. This comprehensive study underscores the efficacy of our combined approach, demonstrating its ability to accurately simulate frustrated quantum spin systems while ensuring computational efficiency.

Introduction. Investigating the intricate and novel physics in quantum many-body systems is a thriving research field in contemporary condensed matter physics. Given the limitations of computational resources, achieving a precise representation of the quantum state is crucial for addressing these challenges. Among the various approaches, tensor network states (TNS) are drawing increasing attention as they offer faithful representations of lowly-entangled quantum states, are free of sign problems, and have been successfully applied to a range of strongly correlated systems over the past decades [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

However, the associated computational cost of TNS escalates extremely fast with the maximum retained state number (DD), commonly referred to as the bond dimension. This issue becomes particularly pronounced, especially in computing the physical observables, such as energy density and correlation functions. Furthermore, since most tensor network algorithms possess iterative structures [7, 8, 4, 6, 5] that cannot be parallelized straightforwardly, the potential of existing acceleration architectures, including CPU multi-core parallelism and GPUs, cannot be explored easily.

On the other hand, Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) [9], belonging to the quantum Monte Carlo family, stands out as another frequently used numerical method in the study of strongly correlated many-body systems [10, 11]. Starting from a prescribed trial wave function |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle, GFMC employs the fixed-node approximation [12] to address the sign problem and leverages the imaginary-time evolution to refine its estimation of the true ground state [13, 14, 11]. The physical observables, including the correlation functions, can be obtained efficiently by importance sampling, and the accuracy can be guaranteed as long as |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle is provided with a certain degree of accuracy of the nodal information in particular.

To take advantage of the high efficiency of Monte Carlo sampling and the sign-free feature of TNS simultaneously, in this study, we propose a hybrid approach [15, 19, 16, 17, 18] that integrates the Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) method with the projected entangled pair state (PEPS) ansatz [20], a specific type of tensor network state which is expected to be able to capture the nodal information of the wave function, to address the general quantum many-body problems. To illustrate the efficacy of this hybrid approach, we focus on the challenging frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on a square lattice. This model is known for the possible existence of quantum spin liquid in the intermediate J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} regime [21, 22, 23, 28, 24, 25, 26, 27, 29, 30] but is difficult for quantum Monte Carlo simulations due to the severe sign problem [31, 32].

As expected, our computational results demonstrate a drastic improvement in the accuracy of ground-state energies, even when employing a preliminary PEPS as the guiding wave function for GFMC [17, 18]. Furthermore, in comparison with the pure PEPS method, which needs to contract a tensor network with bond dimension D2D^{2} in the expectation value calculations (with leading cost D12D^{12} generally) [7, 33, 34], the hybrid approach can fully use the highly efficient Markov chain and importance sampling techniques to expedite the calculations, and the resulting tensor network is of dimension DD only for each physical configurations (with leading cost D6D^{6} and thus can be contracted much more efficiently) [35, 36, 37].

Focusing on the intermediate phases, with periodic boundary conditions, to assess the validity and efficiency, we carefully benchmark the results obtained from the hybrid approach with those obtained from the exact diagonalization, density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), and some other approaches [38, 28, 39, 40, 41]. Besides the energy density, we also calculated the bond correlations and the static spin and dimer structure factors. Finally, we identify a possible columnar valence-bond state (VBS) phase [42] in the intermediate parameter regime about 0.52<J2/J1<0.580.52\textless J_{2}/J_{1}\textless 0.58, and we do not observe a possible nearby quantum spin liquid phase [25, 41] in our calculations.

Model. The frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model is defined by the following Hamiltonian,

H=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j,\displaystyle H={J_{1}}\sum\limits_{\left\langle{i,j}\right\rangle}{{\mathbf{S}_{i}}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{j}}}+{J_{2}}\sum\limits_{\left\langle\left\langle{i,j}\right\rangle\right\rangle}{{\mathbf{S}_{i}}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{j}}}, (1)

where 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} is the spin-1/21/2 angular momentum operator defined at the ii-th site on a square lattice, ⟨…⟩\left\langle{...}\right\rangle and ⟨⟨…⟩⟩\left\langle\left\langle{...}\right\rangle\right\rangle indicate the nearest and next-nearest neighboring summation, respectively. We focus on the case where both J1J_{1} and J2J_{2} are antiferromagnetic and consider system size N=L×LN=L\times L with periodic boundary conditions.

When J1{J_{1}} dominates, the system is in a Neel phase with antiferromagnetic (AFM) long-range order [43, 44], while when J2{J_{2}} dominates, the ground state manifests a well-established collinear AFM phase [45, 46]. Nevertheless, the intermediate regime with J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} around 0.5 remains a subject of considerable debate and scrutiny [47, 48, 21, 49, 50, 51, 22, 23, 28, 24, 25, 52, 26, 53, 27, 54, 29, 30, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 41, 39, 38, 40, 61]. The strong quantum frustration and fluctuations pose a great challenge for numerical simulations. Despite numerous investigations into the characteristics of this regime, including the plaquette VBS [55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 48], the columnar VBS [47, 60, 52], a gapless quantum spin liquid [21, 30, 29, 28], and other proposals [22, 23, 39, 24, 25, 26, 41, 27, 61], the precise nature of this quantum phase remains a topic of controversy. In this study, we always set J1=1{J_{1}}=1 for simplicity.

PEPS guiding wave function. PEPS [20] is a typical tensor network state extensively used to study two-dimensional quantum many-body systems. The PEPS ansatz we used in this study is sketched in Fig. 1 for L=6L=6 and can be formulated in the following

|Ψ⟩=∑{σ}[Tr​∏iTli​ri​ui​di​σi(i)]​|σ1​σ2​…​σi​…⟩,{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{\{\sigma\}}\left[\mathrm{Tr}\prod_{i}T_{l_{i}r_{i}u_{i}d_{i}\sigma_{i}}^{(i)}\right]\big|\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}...\sigma_{i}...\big\rangle,}} (2)

where T(i)T^{(i)} is the local tensor defined at the ii-th site with (li,ri,ui,di)(l_{i},r_{i},u_{i},d_{i}) its link indices and σi\sigma_{i} its local physical configuration, as show in Fig. 1. For any given spin configuration {σ}\{\sigma\}, the superposition coefficient is given by the trace (Tr) in Eq. (2), which denotes the contraction of a two-dimensional tensor network, namely summation over all the link indices of the local tensors. The bond dimension DD, the highest value that the link indices can take, is an important parameter in tensor network states. By increasing DD, the number of parameters and the representation capability can be enhanced, but the computational cost escalates fast too [7, 33]. Therefore, one should make a balance between performance and cost. In our calculations, the bond dimension we focused on is D=4D=4, but near the phase boundary, we have pushed to larger DD (no larger than 7) to check consistency. More background on tensor network states is provided in App. I.

This study considers the PEPS wave function as the trial ground state and guiding wave function for the GFMC calculations below. To generate such a trial state, we first perform energy minimization through variational approach with the help of automatic differentiation technique [62, 63] for the two-dimensional Hamiltonian to get the ground state |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle in the thermodynamic limit [64, 65, 53], and then approximate the guiding wave function |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle of the same Hamiltonian but on a L×LL\times L torus by placing the local tensors of |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle there, as shown in Fig. 1. More details of the preparation of |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle are explained in App. II.

GFMC method. The basic idea of GFMC is simple [10, 11]. Starting from an arbitrary state |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle, it performs the imaginary-time evolution to get the desired ground state |Ψg⟩|\Psi_{g}\rangle, that is

limβ→∞e−β​H^​|Φ0⟩→|Ψg⟩,\lim\limits_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}e^{-\beta\hat{H}}|\Phi_{0}\rangle\rightarrow|\Psi_{g}\rangle, (3)

where the initial trial state satisfies ⟨Φ0|Ψg⟩≠0\langle\Phi_{0}|\Psi_{g}\rangle\neq 0. In practice, the evolution process is divided into many small slices by setting β=M​τ\beta=M\tau with τ\tau a small number, and then the so-called Green’s function is defined as the matrix element of e−τ​H^e^{-\tau\hat{H}}, i.e.,

Gα​γ=⟨α|e−τ​H^|γ⟩≈δα​γ−τ​Hα​γ,\displaystyle G_{\alpha\gamma}=\langle\alpha|e^{-\tau\hat{H}}|\gamma\rangle\approx\delta_{\alpha\gamma}-\tau H_{\alpha\gamma}, (4)

where α\alpha and γ\gamma denote different spin configurations {σ}\{\sigma\}. By normalizing the rows of GG, the element of G~=b−1​G\tilde{G}=b^{-1}G can be considered as the transition amplitude between configurations. Then we can employ a Markov process with the transition matrix G~\tilde{G} to evolve the wave function |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle. Here bb is a diagonal matrix whose nonzero elements bα≡∑γGα​γb_{\alpha}\equiv\sum_{\gamma}G_{\alpha\gamma}. In this study, we choose the PEPS |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle as the initial trial wave function |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle.

In order to improve efficiency, importance sampling is adopted to guide the sampling process. For quantum systems with sign problems, the fixed-node approximation is usually adopted in the GFMC method [12, 11], and an appropriate guiding wave function is expected to circumvent the sign problem, in which one needs to identify the nodes of the guiding wave function and fix them during the whole evolution process of |Φ0⟩|\Phi_{0}\rangle. For this reason, it is crucial to ensure that the guiding wave function can accurately capture the nodal information of the ground state wave function [16, 18]. As mentioned above, we choose a PEPS, |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, as the guiding wave function in our approach. At the beginning, the configurations of the Markov chain follow a distribution characterized by |Φ0|2\left|\Phi_{0}\right|^{2} (in our study, it is also |Ψ0|2\left|\Psi_{0}\right|^{2}), and then it progressively converges to the ground state after a sufficiently long imaginary-time evolution. It is expected that the PEPS wave function can capture the nodal information of the ground state wave functions, even when DD is small, and then GFMC can be used efficiently to refine the wave function and calculate the observables.

Ground State Energy. To show the validity of the hybrid approach, firstly, we focus on a L=6L=6 torus, respectively with J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 and J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55 where the frustration is known to be very strong. We report the ground state energy obtained with different bond dimensions DD in Tab. 1. It shows clearly that for both the J2J_{2} values, the final energies EgE_{g} obtained from the GFMC are indeed lower than the initial values E0E_{0} provided by the PEPS wave function |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, as it should be. Though the ground state energy becomes more and more accurate when DD becomes larger, the GFMC can always improve the PEPS energy further. This reflects the fact that the GFMC method goes beyond variational, and its performance relies significantly on the accuracy of the starting wave function. In this study, we keep D≤7D\leq 7 to balance performance and efficiency.

Tab. 2 and Tab. 3 compare our benchmark results with existing data in the literature for L=6L=6 and L=10L=10, respectively. For L=6L=6 torus, where the exact diagonalization results are available, the hybrid approach can obtain very accurate results with even D=5D=5, which is relatively small. The hybrid approach is better in performance than variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [28] and convolutional neural network (CNN) [40], close to DMRG [39] and improved restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) method [41]. In Fig. 2, we plot the energy EgE_{g} as a function of DD. It shows clearly that the energy can be systematically improved as DD becomes larger, and the extrapolated values in the large-DD limit can be expected to reproduce the exact value accurately [66]. For L=10L=10 torus, the conclusion is similar. Even with D=4D=4, our hybrid approach can provide lower energies than the VMC [28] and CNN [40], and the values coincide very well with those obtained by DMRG calculations [39].

Phase Diagram. To study the ground state phase diagram, we first calculate the magnetization density that is defined in the following

M=⟨Sx⟩2+⟨Sy⟩2+⟨Sz⟩2,\displaystyle M=\sqrt{\langle S^{x}\rangle^{2}+\langle S^{y}\rangle^{2}+\langle S^{z}\rangle^{2}}, (5)

where

Sα=1L2∑i​jSi​jα(−1)n,α=x,y,z\displaystyle S^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{ij}S^{\alpha}_{ij}(-1)^{n},\quad\alpha=x,y,z (6)

Here the subscripts (i​j)(ij) denote that the spin is defined at the ii-th row and the jj-th column of the square lattice. For the antiferromagnetic Neel order parameter, n=i+jn=i+j in Eq. (6), while for the antiferromagnetic collinear order parameter, n=in=i or n=jn=j, depending on how the collinear order stretches in space. As shown in Fig. 3, the Neel magnetization MneelM_{\textrm{neel}} is nonzero when J2J_{2} is small and rapidly decays to roughly zero when J2>0.52J_{2}>0.52. On the other hand, Fig. 4 shows that the collinear magnetization McollM_{\textrm{coll}} is zero when J2J_{2} is small, but escalates fast when J2>0.58J_{2}>0.58. In the intermediate region, about 0.52<J2<0.580.52<J_{2}<0.58, both the two magnetizations are very small, indicating a possible nonmagnetic state.

To unveil the nature of the intermediate phase, we plot the bond correlation ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩\langle{\mathbf{S}_{i}}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{j}}\rangle for each nearest neighbor in Fig. 5 for J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55, where the Neel phase (J2=0J_{2}=0) and collinear phase (J2=1J_{2}=1) are also included for comparison. It shows clearly that different from J2=0J_{2}=0 (Neel phase) and J2=1J_{2}=1 (collinear phase) cases, where lattice translation symmetry for this quantity is conserved, the intermediate phase simultaneously breaks translational symmetry and rotational symmetry. In fact, this phase shows a clear columnar VBS feature along the yy-direction, which can be characterized by a local order parameter Δ\Delta defined as

Δ=2N​(∑i∈even,j⟨𝐒i,j⋅𝐒i+1,j⟩−∑i∈odd,j⟨𝐒i,j⋅𝐒i+1,j⟩)\displaystyle\Delta=\frac{2}{N}\left(\sum_{i\in\textrm{even},j}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i,j}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{i+1,j}}\rangle-\sum_{i\in\textrm{odd},j}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i,j}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{i+1,j}}\rangle\right) (7)

In Fig. 6, we plot its expectation value with respect to J2J_{2}. It shows clearly that this quantity is nonzero only in a narrow region of about 0.52<J2<0.580.52<J_{2}<0.58, which agrees well with what we have concluded from the magnetizations.

Apart from the results of 6×66\times 6 torus, in Fig. 3, Fig. 4, and Fig. 6, we also plot the results for larger clusters up to L=12L=12 as well as extrapolations to the thermodynamic limit. It shows that, when system size becomes larger, MneelM_{\text{neel}}, McollM_{\text{coll}} and Δ\Delta roughly become more stronger in the region of J2<0.52J_{2}<0.52, J2>0.58J_{2}>0.58, and 0.52<J2<0.580.52<J_{2}<0.58, respectively. Results obtained for tori with different sizes give consistent conclusions.

In Fig. 7, we also checked the Neel order parameter MneelM_{\text{neel}} and columnar VBS order parameter Δ\Delta for larger DD, near the boundary between the two phases. It shows that the qualitative conclusion holds for larger DD: when J2>0.52J_{2}>0.52, MneelM_{\text{neel}} rapidly decays to roughly zero and Δ\Delta rises fastly, that is, the columnar VBS order gradually establishes in this region. This verifies our expectation that the PEPS |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle can roughly capture the nodal structure of the true ground state wave function, even when DD is small, and the GFMC method can do further optimization based on this nice feature. Moreover, it shows that when DD becomes larger, the Neel and columnar VBS phases become more stable in the J2<0.52J_{2}<0.52 and 0.52<J2<0.580.52<J_{2}<0.58, respectively. Therefore, together with the finite-size analysis, we find a columnar VBS phase in the intermediate region about 0.52<J2<0.580.52<J_{2}<0.58, and do not observe the possible quantum spin liquid phase between the Neel phase and VBS phase.

To further justify our result, we also calculated the static structure factor S⁡(k)S(k) for spin-spin correlation

S⁡(𝐤)=1N2​∑i,j⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩​ei​𝐤⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j),S\left({\mathbf{k}}\right)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum\limits_{i,j}{\left\langle{\mathbf{S}_{i}}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{j}}\right\rangle}{e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}-{{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}}\right)}}, (8)

and dimer-dimer correlation

Sd,α​(𝐤)=1N2​∑i,j[⟨Di,α​Dj,α⟩−⟨Di,α⟩​⟨Dj,α⟩]​ei​𝐤⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j),S_{d,\alpha}\left({\mathbf{k}}\right)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum\limits_{i,j}\big[\langle{D}_{i,\alpha}{D}_{j,\alpha}\rangle-\langle{D}_{i,\alpha}\rangle\langle{D}_{j,\alpha}\rangle\big]{e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}-{{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}}\right)}}, (9)

where Di,α=𝐒i⋅𝐒i+α^{D}_{i,\alpha}={\mathbf{S}_{i}}\cdot{\mathbf{S}_{i+\hat{\alpha}}} is the bond correlation defined for the ii-th site, where α=x,y\alpha=x,y denotes the two orientations for square lattice.

The structure factors for J2=0.45,0.55,0.65J_{2}=0.45,0.55,0.65 are shown respectively in Fig. 8(a), Fig. 8(b) and Fig. 8(c) in detail. Fig. 8 shows that when J2=0.45J_{2}=0.45, S⁡(𝐤)S({\mathbf{k}}) displays a clear peak at (π,π)(\pi,\pi). Though Sd,x​(𝐤)S_{d,x}({\mathbf{k}}) also develops weak peaks along ky=0k_{y}=0, it does not show clear kxk_{x} dependence. It is likewise with Sd,y​(𝐤)S_{d,y}({\mathbf{k}}). This means that when the ground state is in an antiferromagnetic Neel order, the columnar VBS order is not well-established. When J2=0.55J_{2}=0.55, the S⁡(𝐤)S({\mathbf{k}}) still peaks at (π,π)(\pi,\pi), but its magnitude is much smaller. Meanwhile, Sd,y​(𝐤)S_{d,y}({\mathbf{k}}) shows a clear peak at (0,π)(0,\pi). This means that the Neel order is significantly suppressed and meanwhile the columnar VBS order in yy-direction is well established and dominates in this phase. When J2=0.65J_{2}=0.65, as shown in Fig. 8(c), the S⁡(𝐤)S({\mathbf{k}}) peaks at (0,π)(0,\pi), Sd,x​(𝐤)S_{d,x}({\mathbf{k}}) peaks weakly at (0,0)(0,0), and at the same time Sd,y​(𝐤)S_{d,y}({\mathbf{k}}) shows a clear peak at (0,0)(0,0). All these signatures indicate that the ground state has entered a collinear antiferromagnetic phase, and the bond correlation preserves the translation symmetry. The analysis here coincides well with the pattern sketched in Fig. 5.

The above evolution picture can also be identified in Fig. 9, where we plot the value of the characteristic peaks, i.e., S⁡(π,π)S(\pi,\pi) for Neel order, S⁡(0,π)S(0,\pi) for collinear order, Sd,x​(π,0)S_{d,x}(\pi,0) and Sd,y​(0,π)S_{d,y}(0,\pi) for columnar VBS order, concerning J2J_{2}. To show finite-size effect, we plot the results of L=6L=6 and L=10L=10 together for comparison. It shows clearly that as J2J_{2} becomes larger, the Neel order becomes weaker and weaker while the collinear order gradually develops. The columnar VBS order is established in the intermediate phase, and is consistent with the order parameter analysis. The results from the two tori differ only in small values, and the qualitative conclusion remains the same. More details about the finite-size analysis on the structure factors can be found in App. III.

Summary and discussion. In this study, we propose a hybrid approach that combines the GFMC method with the PEPS ansatz to investigate the ground state phase diagram of the frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model on a square lattice. By utilizing the preliminary PEPS state obtained through automatic differentiation [64, 67] as a guiding wave function for GFMC, the hybrid approach significantly enhances the accuracy of the ground state energy. This supports the argument that the PEPS can accurately characterize the nodal structure of quantum frustrated systems, as also evidenced in previous studies [16, 17]. Furthermore, the GFMC can efficiently give the physical observables, including the correlation functions [18]. Our results, obtained from system sizes up to L=12L=12 and bond dimensions up to D=7D=7, including various order parameters and static structure factors, reveal the presence of a possible columnar VBS phase in the intermediate regime around 0.52<J2<0.580.52\textless J_{2}\textless 0.58. The conclusion is consistent with the previous studies by Schwinger boson approach [60], series expansion [47], and the more recent symmetric infinite PEPS [52]. Though we cannot fully exclude the possibility of the existence of a narrow quantum spin liquid phase [25, 41], we tend to believe that there is no such state between the Neel phase and the VBS phase from the finite-size and finite-D analysis on the order parameters.

The hybrid approach capitalizes on the PEPS’ capability of characterizing the nodal structure of quantum many-body states and the full parallelizability of Monte Carlo sampling. Specifically, given the PEPS guiding wave function with bond dimension DD, the hybrid method can further optimize it with computational cost scales as n​D6nD^{6}, where nn is the number of spin configurations sampled in the GFMC, and D6D^{6} comes from the evaluation of ⟨{σ}|Ψ⟩\langle\{\sigma\}|\Psi\rangle for a given {σ}\{\sigma\}. While PEPS with a larger DD is expected to capture a more accurate nodal structure, nn should increase with LL but can be parallelized completely. Consequently, more computational resources directly translate to enhanced results. For instance, employing larger DD, e.g., through the nested tensor network technique [33, 34], and more accurate trial states for frustrated systems with finite size, e.g., using other tensor network ansatz like projected entangled simplex state [68] and energy minimization at finite size directly, increasing system size, and augmenting the number of samples can further refine the outcomes and provide a clearer understanding of the intermediate phase, such as the exact boundaries of the VBS phase and the nature of the transition between this VBS and the Neel phase [69]. We would like to leave these topics as future pursuits.

Appendix

In this appendix, we provide more background on the tensor network states, more details on the guiding wave function preparation, and more finite-size analysis of the static structure factors.

I. More background on tensor network states

The PEPS wave function, a cornerstone of our research, is a widely used tensor network state in the study of quantum many-body physics [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. The two important features of PEPS and many other tensor network states are area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy and the absence of negative sign problem.

The area-law scaling originates from its specific dense structure [7], i.e., any bipartition of the physical degrees of freedom in a PEPS will inevitably cut multiple links/bonds whose number is proportional to the system size, and this is quite different from other one-dimensional wave function ansatz like matrix product state.

The general statement that the tensor network state is free of the sign problem [1, 8, 5, 6] stems from the fact that tensor network algorithms are usually based on the idea of the renormalization group, and the concept of probability of a given configuration, like in quantum Monte Carlo, is not touched directly. For example, when tensor networks are used to study a quantum lattice model, the main task is to determine the tensor network state representation of the target quantum state [20, 7], such as the ground state, and the strategies to achieve this include energy minimization or imaginary-time evolution. While performing the strategies and later in the expectation value calculations, the work needs to be done is to contract tensor networks approximately through some renormalization-group-based techniques, such as boundary matrix product state or corner transfer matrix renormalization group [7, 6, 70], etc. In the entire process mentioned above, the concept of probability is not touched at all. Even in the imaginary-time evolution, which can be regarded as the counterpart of the path integral, the only thing one needs to do is to update the wave function by variational approaches or some singular-value-decomposition-based techniques [71] instead of evaluating e−τ​He^{-\tau H} itself. Therefore, in this sense, the problem of negative probability for a given basis is avoided completely, and it is similar to the case of variational Monte Carlo or any other wave-function-based methods. That is why it is generally said that the tensor network state is free of sign problems. There are many successful applications of TNS in systems that have sign problems for Monte Carlo, such as kagome spin liquid [68], Shastry-Sutherland model [72], lattice gauge theory with finite density [73], Hubbard [74] and tt-JJ model [75], etc.

The bond dimension DD is an important hyper-parameter to control the number of variational parameters in the tensor network state ansatz. For example, for the PEPS defined on a L×LL\times L torus like in Fig. 1, if no translational symmetry is used, then the total number of parameters is L2​D4​dL^{2}D^{4}d, where dd is the dimension of the local Hilbert space extended by σi\sigma_{i}.

Physically, the PEPS wave function can be understood in terms of maximally entangled states of some auxiliary systems, as originally proposed in Refs. [20, 76]. The idea is illustrated in Fig. 10. Firstly, one can arrange four auxiliary virtual particles around each lattice site, and let every two virtual particles on the same link form a maximally entangled paired state, e.g., |ω⟩=∑i=1D|i,i⟩|\omega\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{D}|i,i\rangle, where |i=1,2,…D⟩|i=1,2,...D\rangle characterizes the specific quantum state of the virtual particles. Then the final state is obtained by applying a projector (namely linear map) P at each lattice site to map the space extended by the four virtual particles to the physical Hilbert space. Therefore, in this sense, DD actually represents the dimension of the auxiliary virtual systems.

Generally, the PEPS ansatz can be more accurate when DD becomes larger, but unfortunately, the computational cost of determining and evaluating the state can scale as D12D^{12} and increase extremely fast [7, 33]. Therefore, as mentioned in the main text, one needs to balance the performance and the cost.

II. Preparation of |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle

This section provides more details about the preparation of guiding PEPS wave function |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle. As mentioned in the main text, the PEPS ansatz is optimized for systems in the thermodynamic limit for simplicity. To be specific, we mainly follow the procedures below:

(1) Choose a supercell with size 2×22\times 2, the smallest size necessary to distinguish the four possible phases of this model. As illustrated in Fig. 11(a), this means there are four distinct tensors in the supercell (denoted as different colors), say {Ta,Tb,Tc,Td}\{T_{a},T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\}, each of which is a tensor with shape D×D×D×D×2D\times D\times D\times D\times 2 and initialized arbitrarily.

(2) The supercell is duplicated and arranged periodically to construct the PEPS ansatz |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle in the thermodynamic limit. Here, the subscript ’2D’ addresses the thermodynamic limit of a two-dimensional lattice. In this case, only four different local tensors are constructing |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle, i.e., {Ta,Tb,Tc,Td}\{T_{a},T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\}. See Fig. 11(b).

(3) Find the optimal {Ta,Tb,Tc,Td}\{T_{a},T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\} which can minimize the ground state energy E=⟨Ψ2​D|H|Ψ2​D⟩⟨Ψ2​D|Ψ2​D⟩E=\frac{\langle\Psi_{2D}|H|\Psi_{2D}\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{2D}|\Psi_{2D}\rangle}. This can be achieved by optimizing them from their initial values through the gradient-based optimization method, such as the L-BFGS quasi-Newton method [77], as long as their gradients, i.e., {∂E∂Ta,∂E∂Tb,∂E∂Tc,∂E∂Td}\{\frac{\partial E}{\partial T_{a}},\frac{\partial E}{\partial T_{b}},\frac{\partial E}{\partial T_{c}},\frac{\partial E}{\partial T_{d}}\} are known. Fortunately, these gradients can be effectively obtained by the so-called automatic differentiation (AD) technique, which essentially uses the backpropagation (i.e., chain rule of derivatives) to calculate the gradients [62, 63]. Therefore, from the arbitrarily initialized {Ta,Tb,Tc,Td}\{T_{a},T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\}, one can calculate the energy EE, and then the AD package [78] can effectively obtain their gradients, which can be used in the L-BFGS method to update these local tensors, and |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle is thus updated in the direction of lower energy. This update procedure can be repeated until some convergence is reached, and then we obtain a PEPS representation |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle of the ground state wave function with some accuracy.

(4) When |Ψ2​D⟩|\Psi_{2D}\rangle is obtained, in order to combine with the GFMC method, we use the obtained supercell to approximately construct the ground state wave function of the same Hamiltonian but on a L×LL\times L torus. Again, this is done by duplicating the supercell and arranging them periodically on a torus [79]. Then finally, the trial PEPS wave function |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle is obtained and can be used as the guiding wave function of the GFMC method. See Fig. 11(c).

The AD technique lies in the heart of the backpropagation algorithm in training neural networks [80], relates closely to the second renormalization group in optimizing a tensor network [64], thus servers as the computational engine of modern deep learning applications and differential programming tensor networks. The basic idea is the chain rule of derivative. For simplicity, we introduce notation T→0\vec{T}_{0} to denote the initial {Ta,Tb,Tc,Td}\{T_{a},T_{b},T_{c},T_{d}\} vectorized and stacked as a single vector. Suppose in order to evaluate the evaluation of the energy, a series of intermediate results {T→1,T→2,…,T→m}\{\vec{T}_{1},\vec{T}_{2},...,\vec{T}_{m}\} are generated sequentially, e.g., in the corner transfer matrix renormalization group algorithm, then the gradient can be calculated through

∂E∂T→0=∂E∂T→m​∂T→m∂T→m−1​∂T→m−1∂T→m−2​…​∂T→2∂T→1​∂T→1∂T→0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial E}{\partial\vec{T}_{0}}=\frac{\partial E}{\partial\vec{T}_{m}}\frac{\partial\vec{T}_{m}}{\partial\vec{T}_{m-1}}\frac{\partial\vec{T}_{m-1}}{\partial\vec{T}_{m-2}}...\frac{\partial\vec{T}_{2}}{\partial\vec{T}_{1}}\frac{\partial\vec{T}_{1}}{\partial\vec{T}_{0}}. (10)

There are well-developed AD packages [78] to perform this reversed mode calculation effectively. For more details about this technique in tensor networks, one can refer to, e.g., Refs. [64, 67].

III. More detailed finite-size analysis on the static structure factors

In Fig. 9 in the main text, we show only the data obtained on 6×66\times 6 and 10×1010\times 10 tori in order to clarify the plot. In this section, we provide more data about the finite-size analysis for each structure factor separately. The results of S⁡(π,π)S(\pi,\pi) (relevant to the antiferromagnetic Neel phase), S⁡(0,π)S(0,\pi) (relevant to the antiferromagnetic collinear phase), Sd,y​(0,π)S_{d,y}(0,\pi) and Sd,x​(π,0)S_{d,x}(\pi,0) (relevant to the columnar VBS phase) are shown in Fig. 12, Fig. 13, Fig. 14 and Fig. 15, respectively. The extrapolations to the thermodynamic limit obtained by a direct power fitting are also included. It shows that although some slight finite-size effect exists, the peak structure of all four quantities remains the same as LL becomes larger. Significantly, the Sd,y​(0,π)S_{d,y}(0,\pi) and Sd,x​(π,0)S_{d,x}(\pi,0) show apparent peaks in the intermediate region consistently and evidence the possible existence of a columnar VBS phase.
